2|in Patients With Chronic Low Back Pain
3|A Randomized Clinical Trial
4|Matthew K. Bagg, PhD; Benedict M. Wand, PhD; Aidan G. Cashin, PhD; Hopin Lee, PhD; Markus Hübscher, PhD;

8|IMPORTANCE The effects of altered neural processing, defined as altering neural networks
9|responsible for perceptions of pain and function, on chronic pain remains unclear.
10|OBJECTIVE To estimate the effect of a graded sensorimotor retraining intervention
11|(RESOLVE) on pain intensity in people with chronic low back pain.
12|DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This parallel, 2-group, randomized clinical trial recruited
13|participants with chronic (>3 months) nonspecific low back pain from primary care and
14|community settings. A total of 276 adults were randomized (in a 1:1 ratio) to the intervention
15|or sham procedure and attention control groups delivered by clinicians at a medical research
16|institute in Sydney, Australia. The first participant was randomized on December 10, 2015,
17|and the last was randomized on July 25, 2019. Follow-up was completed on February 3, 2020.
18|INTERVENTIONS Participants randomized to the intervention group (n = 138) were asked to
19|participate in 12 weekly clinical sessions and home training designed to educate them about
20|and assist them with movement and physical activity while experiencing lower back pain.
21|Participants randomized to the control group (n = 138) were asked to participate in 12 weekly
22|clinical sessions and home training that required similar time as the intervention but did not
23|focus on education, movement, and physical activity. The control group included sham laser
24|and shortwave diathermy applied to the back and sham noninvasive brain stimulation.
25|MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The primary outcome was pain intensity at 18 weeks,
26|measured on an 11-point numerical rating scale (range, 0 [no pain] to 10 [worst pain
27|imaginable]) for which the between-group minimum clinically important difference
28|is 1.0 point.
29|RESULTS Among 276 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 46 [14.3] years; 138 [50%]
30|women), 261 (95%) completed follow-up at 18 weeks. The mean pain intensity was 5.6 at
31|baseline and 3.1 at 18 weeks in the intervention group and 5.8 at baseline and 4.0 at 18 weeks
32|in the control group, with an estimated between-group mean difference at 18 weeks
33|of -1.0 point ([95% CI, -1.5 to -0.4]; P = .001), favoring the intervention group.
34|CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this randomized clinical trial conducted at a single center
35|among patients with chronic low back pain, graded sensorimotor retraining, compared with a
36|sham procedure and attention control, significantly improved pain intensity at 18 weeks. The
37|improvements in pain intensity were small, and further research is needed to understand the
38|generalizability of the findings.

2|n 2019, low back pain affected approximately 52 million
3|peopleintheUSand568millionpeopleworldwide.1,2Based
4|on data from 1990 to 2019, low back pain was the leading
5|cause of years lived with disability worldwide.1 A meta-
6|analysis from 2013 indicated that one-third of people with low
7|back pain experienced persistent pain and disability 3 months
8|after symptom onset,3 and these individuals were unlikely to
9|recover completely within 1 year.3
10|New effective treatments are needed for low back pain.4-6
11|Graded sensorimotor retraining (RESOLVE) is a novel inter-
12|vention designed to alter how people think about their body
13|in pain, how they process sensory information from their back,
14|and how they move their back during activities.
15|This randomized clinical trial evaluated the effects of
16|graded sensorimotor retraining, compared with an attention
17|control with sham procedure, in people with moderate to se-
18|vere chronic low back pain.
19|Methods
20|Study Design and Participants
21|This parallel, 2-group, randomized clinical trial was ap-
22|proved by the University of New South Wales Human Re-
23|searchEthicsCommittee(HC15357).Thetrialprotocolisshown
24|in Supplement 1. Protocols published during the trial7,8 did not
25|include secondary outcomes that were process variables, and
26|these outcomes are not reported here. The secondary out-
27|come of Insomnia Severity Index was omitted from the pub-
28|lished protocol7 in error. Participants were recruited between
29|November 1, 2015, and July 28, 2019. The first participant was
30|randomized on December 10, 2015, and follow-up was com-
31|pleted on February 3, 2020. All participants gave written in-
32|formed consent.
33|Participants were recruited in Sydney, Australia, by di-
34|rect referral from primary care clinicians as well as by adver-
35|tisements in the community using local and online media.
36|People were eligible for inclusion if they reported back pain
37|with a pain intensity rating of at least 3 of 10 on an 11-point nu-
38|merical rating scale that persisted for at least 12 consecutive
39|weeks, regardless of whether they had associated leg pain. Ad-
40|ditional inclusion criteria were age between 18 and 70 years,
41|fluency in the English language, ability to access the internet,
42|and availability of a trusted person to assist with the home por-
43|tion of the intervention. People with radicular pain, with low
44|back pain caused by a serious medical condition (ie, infec-
45|tion, fracture, malignancy), who were pregnant or gave birth
46|in the past 6 months, who had undergone spinal surgery in the
47|past 12 months or were scheduled for major surgery in the next
48|12 months, with an uncontrolled mental health condition that
49|would impede participation, and with contraindications to
50|physical activity, transcranial direct current stimulation, cra-
51|nialelectricalstimulation,low-intensitylasertherapy,orshort-
52|wave diathermy were excluded.
53|Randomization and Masking
54|Eligible participants were randomly allocated (in a 1:1 ratio) to
55|receive the intervention or matched attention control with
56|sham procedures. Participants were informed that both group
57|interventions contained treatments that targeted central ner-
58|vous system function, combined with treatments directed to-
59|ward functioning of the back. Participants were informed that
60|some of the treatments were not active. No further informa-
61|tion was disclosed publicly to maintain the integrity of blind-
62|ing. Participants were not required to stop ongoing treatment
63|for their low back pain.
64|Arandomizationsequencewasgeneratedusingcomputer-
65|generatedblockrandomization(randomblocksizerange,2-10).
66|Randomizations were sealed in opaque, sequentially num-
67|bered envelopes. Eligible participants were randomly as-
68|signed immediately after baseline assessment by opening the
69|next numbered envelope, at which point they were consid-
70|ered enrolled. The trial clinicians were unblinded, but partici-
71|pants, researchers collecting outcome data, and researchers
72|analyzing outcome data were masked to group identity.
73|Procedures
74|Graded Sensorimotor Retraining
75|The graded sensorimotor retraining intervention was deliv-
76|ered by a physiotherapist (n = 6) or an exercise physiologist
77|(n = 1). The intervention consisted of 12 individual treatment
78|sessions lasting up to 1 hour scheduled over 12 to 18 weeks.
79|The intervention included a home treatment component that
80|participants were encouraged to complete for 30 minutes 5
81|times per week during the treatment period, recording their
82|participation in an intervention diary. The primary intention
83|wastohelppeopleinpainunderstandthatitwassafeandhelp-
84|ful to move (step 1), feel safe to move (step 2), and experience
85|that it was safe to move (step 3) as they progressed toward re-
86|engagement with meaningful functional goals. The first ses-
87|sion included contemporary pain education delivered using
88|graphical media, video, metaphor, and narrative and contin-
89|ued for the duration of the intervention (step 1). In sessions 2
90|through 12, graded premovement treatments were provided
91|in the clinic and continued at home, which involved sensory
92|precision training and mental rehearsal of movement (step 2).
93|Inthesixthsession,participantsbegangradedmovementtrain-
94|ing in the clinic and continued at home, starting with simple
95|Key Points
96|Question What is the effect of a graded sensorimotor retraining
97|intervention on pain intensity for adults with chronic low back pain?
98|Findings In this randomized clinical trial that included 276
99|participants, a graded sensorimotor retraining intervention,
100|compared with a sham procedure and attention control, resulted
101|in a statistically significant improvement in pain intensity at 18
102|weeks (estimated mean difference, 1.0 point on an 11-point
103|numeric rating scale [range, 0-10 points]).
104|Meaning Among patients with chronic low back pain, a graded
105|sensorimotor retraining intervention, compared with a sham
106|procedure and attention control, significantly improved pain
107|intensity at 18 weeks, although the improvements were modest
108|and further research in other patient populations is needed to
109|understand the generalizability of the findings.

7|Attention Control With Sham Procedures
8|The attention control with sham procedures was delivered by
9|a physiotherapist (n = 3), 2 of whom also delivered the graded

16|The first 2 sessions included discussion of the partici-
17|pant's low back pain experience without advice or education
18|provided. Sessions 3 through 12 included sham low-intensity
19|laser therapy to the most painful area of the back and sham
20|transcranial direct current stimulation applied to the motor
21|and prefrontal cortices on the side contralateral to their worst
22|pain.9 In the sixth session, participants began sham short-
23|wave diathermy over the back, which continued for the dura-
24|tion of the intervention. To match the intervention's home
25|training component, participants were provided with a sham
26|cranial electrical stimulation device and instructed to use it
27|at home for 30 minutes 5 times a week and record their use in
28|a diary. Treatment adherence to the intervention and control
29|was assessed by recording the attendance of participants at
30|each treatment session.
31|Data Collection
32|Data were collected at baseline (prior to randomization) and
33|at 18, 26, and 52 weeks after randomization using mailed ques-
34|tionnaires and secure online data-capture software. Demo-
35|graphic and clinical characteristics (age, sex, work status, edu-
36|cational level, duration of current back pain episode, number
37|of previous episodes, self-reported use of prescribed and over-
38|the-counter medicines for low back pain, other areas of pain,
39|and back pain-related compensation status) were obtained at
40|the baseline assessment prior to randomization, along with all
41|primary and secondary outcome measurements. No data were
42|collected on race, ethnicity, or ancestry.
43|Outcome Measurements
44|Primary Outcome
45|The primary outcome was mean pain intensity over the pre-
46|vious week assessed using an 11-point numerical rating
47|scale10 (range, 0 [no pain] to 10 [worst pain imaginable]) at 18
48|weeks after randomization. The between-group minimal
49|clinically important difference (MCID) is 1.0 point on the
50|11-point numerical rating scale.11 The within-group MCID is
51|a 30% change from baseline.12
52|Secondary Outcomes
53|Secondary outcomes were disability, assessed using the 24-
54|item Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire13 (scale range,
55|0-24; higher scores indicate greater disability; within-group
56|MCID, 30% from baseline)12; health-related quality of life, as-
57|sessed using the 5-level EuroQoL-5 dimensions14 question-
58|naire (EQ-5D-5L; scale range, 1-5; higher scores indicate bet-

64|higher scores indicate worse outcome; MCID not estab-
65|lished); sleep quality (insomnia), assessed using the Insom-
66|nia Severity Index (range 0-28; higher scores indicate worse
67|insomnia; MCID not established); beliefs about low back pain,
68|assessed using the Back Beliefs Questionnaire (range 9-45;
69|lower scores indicate more pessimistic beliefs about the con-
70|sequences of low back pain; MCID not established); kinesio-
71|phobia, assessed using the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia
72|(range, 17-68; higher scores are worse; MCID not estab-
73|lished); catastrophizing, assessed using the Pain Catastroph-
74|izing Scale (range, 0-52; higher scores are worse; MCID not es-
75|tablished); the Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire (range, 0-60;
76|higher scores are better; within-group MCID, 5.5); and treat-
77|ment rationale credibility, assessed using the Credibility and
78|Expectancy Questionnaire16 (scale range, 0-48; lower scores
79|are worse, MCID not established).
80|Serious adverse events and adverse events were reported
81|by the patient and recorded by the trial therapist at the begin-
82|ning of each treatment session.
83|Additional Prespecified Outcomes
84|Additional prespecified outcomes consist of process variables
85|(2-pointdiscriminationdistance,left-rightjudgementtaskper-
86|formance [accuracy and speed], Neurophysiology of Pain
87|Questionnaire score, Fremantle Back Awareness Question-
88|naire score, Movement Imagery Questionnaire-Revised score,
89|and Elgueta-Cancino Pelvic Tilt Test) and cost-effectiveness,
90|which will be reported separately.
91|Post Hoc Outcomes
92|Post hoc outcomes consisted of recovery, defined as pain in-
93|tensity in the past week rated less than or equal to 1 on the
94|11-point numerical rating scale at both 18 and 26 weeks after
95|randomization (MCID not established); response to interven-
96|tion, defined as at least 30% reduction in pain intensity from
97|baseline to 18 weeks; response to intervention, defined as at
98|least50%reductioninpainintensityfrombaselineto18weeks;

100|Recovery Scale (range, -5 to 5; lower scores indicate poorer re-
101|covery; MCID not established).

14|Statistical Analysis
15|Mean values are presented for normally distributed data and
16|median values with IQRs are presented for skewed data. The
17|mean between-group difference on the primary outcome of
18|pain intensity and the secondary outcomes of disability, qual-
19|ity of life, depressive symptoms, insomnia, back beliefs,
20|kinesiophobia, pain catastrophizing, pain self-efficacy, and
21|global perceived effect were estimated with linear mixed mod-
22|elsthatincorporatedgrouprandomization,time,andthetreat-
23|ment × time interaction term. Time was modeled as a 4-level
24|categorical variable, which assumed observations were col-
25|lected at the stipulated time. The model was robust to data
26|missing at random and accounted for baseline outcome val-
27|ues. For continuous outcomes, the estimated effects were the
28|differences in mean values between the groups at 18 weeks,
29|26 weeks, and 52 weeks and the overall difference across all
30|time points. For the post hoc dichotomous outcomes, recov-
31|eryandresponse,thepercentageofparticipantsineithergroup
32|was compared using the Fisher exact test. The effect of the in-
33|terventionwasexpressedastheabsolutedifferenceinrisk,and
34|the ratio of risks, between groups. Credibility was compared
35|between groups using an independent samples t test. The full
36|analysis set included all randomized participants who pro-
37|vided data at each time point analyzed. For all statistical analy-
38|ses, participant data were analyzed in the groups to which they
39|were randomized, regardless of adherence. Missing data were

3|Abstract
4|Background: Statistical analysis plans describe the planned data management and analysis for clinical
5|trials. This supports transparent reporting and interpretation of clinical trial results. This paper reports the
6|statistical analysis plan for the RESOLVE clinical trial. The RESOLVE trial assigned participants with
7|chronic low back pain to graded sensory-motor precision training or sham-control.
8|Results: We report the planned data management and analysis for the primary and secondary outcomes.
9|The primary outcome is pain intensity at 18-weeks post randomisation. We will use mixed-effects models
10|to analyse the primary and secondary outcomes by intention-to-treat. We will report adverse effects in full.
11|We also describe analyses if there is non-adherence to the interventions, data management procedures and
12|our planned reporting of results.
13|Conclusion: This statistical analysis plan will minimise the potential for bias in the analysis and reporting
14|of results from the RESOLVE trial.

3|Introduction
4|Background and rationale
5|Low back pain is a burdensome and disabling health condition.1,2 People who experience low back pain for
6|longer than three months have a low chance of recovery and experience substantial functional and financial
7|difficulty.3210 Results of clinical trials of contemporary interventions indicate that, on average, people with
8|persistent low back pain experience small to no benefit, compared to control. Accordingly, there is an
9|urgent need to develop more effective interventions.
10|Recent progress in understanding the role of the central nervous system (CNS) in the low back pain
11|experience bears promise for the development of new treatment approaches. Accumulating data indicate
12|that people with persistent low back pain have differences in CNS structure, function, and biochemistry;
13|compared to people without pain.11220 Research has demonstrated that these differences may be related to
14|aspects of the low back pain experience.21223
15|Interventions designed to target the CNS (termed herein, psychophysical interventions) have been
16|developed and tested in a number of small studies.24227 Further research has combined these new
17|interventions with traditional interventions directed towards functioning of the back, or psychological
18|aspects of the pain experience. These data suggest that there may be additional benefit from a combined
19|approach.28232 Work is underway to evaluate these treatment programs in adequately powered,
20|prospectively registered, randomised controlled trials.33235
21|Aim
22|The aim of the RESOLVE Trial is to evaluate the effectiveness of a psychophysical-traditional intervention
23|(graded sensory-motor precision training) compared to a sham intervention for reducing pain intensity for
24|people with persistent low back pain at 18-weeks post-randomisation. This statistical analysis plan reports
25|the planned analyses of primary and secondary outcomes.
26|Study Methods
27|Trial design
28|The RESOLVE Trial is a two-group, parallel, randomised clinical trial with 1:1 allocation. Participants and
29|outcome assessors are blinded to group allocation and study hypotheses.33
30|Eligibility
31|We defined these eligibility criteria in the trial protocol:33

38|Conclusions
39|In this randomized clinical trial conducted at a single center
40|among patients with chronic low back pain, graded senso-
41|rimotor retraining, compared with a sham procedure and at-
42|tention control, significantly improved pain intensity at 18
43|weeks. The improvements in pain intensity were small, and
44|further research is needed to understand the generalizability
45|of the findings.
